lessons.title: Electronic Systems and the Input-Process-Output Model
lessons.description: How electronic systems use sensors, processors and outputs to control products.
lessons.content_html:
How Electronic Systems Work

Electronic systems are at the heart of almost every modern product — from a bedside lamp that dims automatically to a fire alarm that wakes a building. Rather than thinking about individual wires and components, designers use a systems approach to plan how a product will function. This means dividing any electronic product into three linked stages: input, process and output. Understanding this model is essential for answering questions about how electronic products detect, decide and respond.

The Input–Process–Output Model

The input–process–output (IPO) model describes all electronic systems. The three stages always occur in this sequence:

  • Input — a sensor or switch detects a change in the environment and converts it into an electrical signal. Examples include a light-dependent resistor detecting low light, or a microswitch being pressed by a moving part.
  • Process — a processor (such as a transistor circuit or microcontroller) receives the signal and decides what to do. It may compare the input against a set threshold and trigger a response only when a condition is met.
  • Output — the system produces a visible, audible or physical response. Common output devices include LEDs, buzzers, motors and display screens.
Key Fact

Every electronic system has three stages: input (sensor detects a change), process (circuit or microcontroller decides) and output (device responds). No electronic product exists that skips one of these stages.

Input Sensors

Sensors are the ‘senses’ of an electronic system. They convert a physical change in the environment into a changing electrical signal. The most commonly tested sensors are:

  • Light-dependent resistor (LDR) — its resistance is high in darkness and falls as light intensity increases. A street lamp controller uses an LDR so the lamp switches on at dusk and off at dawn.
  • Thermistor — a thermistor has high resistance at low temperatures and low resistance when warm. A central heating thermostat uses a thermistor to detect when the room drops below the set temperature.
  • Microswitch — a mechanical switch with a small lever; a tiny force triggers it. Printers use microswitches to detect when a paper tray is open.
  • Moisture sensor — two conductive tracks separated by a gap; when water bridges the gap, current flows, completing the circuit. A plant-watering alert uses this type. Important: simply naming “moisture sensor” is not enough in the exam — you must explain that water completes the circuit between the two tracks, changing the current flowing to the processor.

Sensors produce either analogue or digital signals. An analogue signal varies continuously — the output of a thermistor changes smoothly as temperature rises. A digital signal is either on or off: a microswitch is either pressed (1) or not pressed (0). Most microcontrollers work in the digital domain, so analogue signals from sensors like LDRs are converted using an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) before the processor can act on them.

Understanding this distinction matters for exam questions asking you to explain how a sensor interfaces with a microcontroller. A thermistor gives a continuously varying voltage; the ADC samples this many times per second and converts each sample into a binary number the processor can compare against a stored threshold value.

Output Devices

The output stage converts the electrical signal back into a physical form the user can see, hear or feel:

  • LED (light-emitting diode) — emits light when current flows in the correct direction. Used as indicator lights, display digits and, increasingly, as the primary light source in products such as cycle lamps.
  • Buzzer — converts electrical pulses into sound via a vibrating disc. Common in alarms, timers and door entry systems.
  • Motor — converts electrical energy into rotary motion. Used to move conveyor belts, open automatic doors and drive robotic arms.
  • Relay — an electromagnetic switch allowing a low-current circuit to control a high-current device safely, such as a microcontroller switching a mains-voltage motor.
Key Fact

An LDR has high resistance in darkness and low resistance in bright light — the opposite of what many students expect. A thermistor has high resistance when cold and low resistance when hot. Getting these directions wrong is the most common error in sensor questions.

Block Diagrams and Circuit Diagrams

Designers use two main types of diagram to represent electronic systems:

  • Block diagram — shows the function of each stage as a labelled box connected by arrows. It does not show individual components or wiring. A block diagram for a security light might show: [LDR] → [Processor] → [LED array].
  • Circuit diagram — shows every component using standard British Standard (BS) symbols and the wiring between them. More detailed than a block diagram and used by engineers building the product.

A basic IPO system runs in one direction: input → process → output. A more advanced system uses feedback to make the output self-correcting. In a closed-loop system, the output is monitored and compared to a desired value; any difference (error) is used to adjust the process. A central heating system is a classic example: the thermistor measures room temperature (feedback), the controller compares it to the target, and the boiler fires or cuts off accordingly.

In contrast, an open-loop system has no feedback: a toaster with only a timer heats for a fixed period regardless of whether the bread is actually toasted. Open-loop systems are simpler and cheaper but less accurate. Closed-loop systems cost more but respond dynamically to changing conditions, making them preferable in safety-critical applications such as industrial robots and medical devices.

Flowcharts

A flowchart maps the logical steps in a control system. Standard shapes are used: ovals for start/stop, rectangles for process steps, diamonds for decisions (with yes/no branches). A flowchart for an automatic night-light would show: Start → Is it dark? (No → loop back; Yes → Turn LED on) → loop back to check again. Flowcharts are particularly useful for describing how a programmable component such as a microcontroller responds to sensor inputs.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to explain how a sensor detects a change, always name the sensor, state what physical quantity it detects, and describe the mechanism — for example, “the LDR’s resistance falls as light intensity increases, lowering the voltage at the processor’s input pin, which triggers the output.” Naming ‘a light sensor’ without the mechanism of detection will score zero on explain questions. For 3-mark ‘Describe’ questions about a system, use three separate sentences: one per IPO stage, each with a named component.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • All electronic systems follow the input–process–output model: a sensor detects a change, a processor makes a decision, and an output device responds.
  • Common input sensors include LDRs (light), thermistors (temperature) and microswitches (physical contact). LDR resistance is high in darkness; thermistor resistance is high when cold.
  • Closed-loop systems use feedback to compare the output against a target and self-correct; open-loop systems have no feedback and cannot adapt to changing conditions.

practice_questions.text:
Which component would be most suitable as the input device in an automatic security light that switches on at dusk?
A) Buzzer
B) LED
C) Light-dependent resistor
D) Motor
practice_questions.marks: C) Light-dependent resistor [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the three stages of the input-process-output model.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for any two correctly named stages; 2 marks for all three: input, process, output. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a thermistor is used as part of an electronic control system for a greenhouse heater.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• The thermistor is connected in the input stage of the circuit and its resistance changes with temperature.
• When the greenhouse temperature falls, the thermistor's resistance increases, raising the voltage at the processor's input.
• The processor detects this change and switches on the heater (output device) to warm the greenhouse. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a moisture sensor detects when a plant pot needs watering and communicates this to the rest of the system.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The moisture sensor has two conductive tracks separated by a small gap in the soil.
• When the soil is dry, there is no electrical path between the tracks and no current flows to the processor.
• When the soil is moist, water bridges the gap, completing the circuit and allowing current to flow.
• The processor detects this current change and triggers an output device (e.g. LED indicator or buzzer) to alert the user.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a closed-loop and an open-loop electronic control system. Use an example of each in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• An open-loop system has no feedback — the output runs for a fixed time or at a fixed level regardless of the result. Example: a timer-controlled toaster runs for a set period whether or not the bread is toasted.
• A closed-loop system continuously monitors the output and feeds this information back to the processor to adjust the system's behaviour. Example: a central heating thermostat uses a thermistor to measure room temperature and cuts off the boiler when the target temperature is reached.
• Open-loop systems are simpler and cheaper to manufacture; closed-loop systems are more precise and suitable for safety-critical applications.
[6 marks — Mastering: Both types explained with accurate examples and a developed comparison of advantages. Secure: Both types named and explained with examples but comparison limited. Developing: One type explained clearly; second type superficial. Emerging: Partial or confused identification of one type.]

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating an automatic door opener for a supermarket entrance. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using an electronic sensor-based system rather than a manual push-button to control the door.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
• A sensor-based system (e.g. infrared motion sensor) responds automatically without the user touching anything, improving accessibility for wheelchair users and those carrying bags.
• The system can be programmed to detect multiple inputs simultaneously (e.g. door position sensor + motion sensor) for greater safety.
• Automatic systems reduce wear on manual hardware over time and can be updated by reprogramming without physical changes.
Disadvantages:
• Electronic systems are more expensive to design, install and maintain than a simple push-button.
• Sensor malfunctions (e.g. false triggers from sunlight or small animals) can cause doors to open inappropriately, creating security or energy-efficiency issues.
• Power dependency means the door fails to open during power cuts unless a battery backup is fitted, which adds further cost.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages, including context of the supermarket entrance. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages identified with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided response or very superficial points.]

lessons.title: Programmable Components and Microcontrollers
lessons.description: How microcontrollers and PICs replace fixed circuits with flexible, reprogrammable control.
lessons.content_html:
Why Use Programmable Components?

Traditional electronic circuits are designed to do one thing. Change the task and you change the circuit — which means redesigning the hardware and going back to manufacture. Programmable components solve this problem. They allow engineers to change what a circuit does simply by loading a different program, with no change to the physical components. This makes products cheaper to develop, easier to update and more versatile — a significant commercial advantage for any manufacturer.

Microcontrollers and PICs

The most important type of programmable component in GCSE Design and Technology is the microcontroller. A microcontroller contains:

  • A processor (CPU) — executes the instructions in the program, performing calculations and making decisions.
  • Memory — stores the program (in non-volatile flash memory, so it survives power loss) and temporary working data (in RAM).
  • Input/output (I/O) pins — connect to sensors, switches, LEDs, motors and other peripheral devices. Pins can be individually configured as inputs or outputs.

A PIC (Programmable Interface Controller) is a popular family of microcontroller chip. PICs are small, low-cost and low-power, making them ideal for embedding in consumer products such as washing machines, microwave ovens and children’s toys. A PIC is programmed by writing code on a computer and then uploading it to the chip via a programmer device.

Key Fact

A microcontroller contains a processor, memory and I/O pins on a single chip. It can read sensor inputs, make decisions according to its program, and control output devices — replacing a large number of separate electronic components with a single programmable unit.

Interfacing with Inputs and Outputs

A microcontroller sits at the process stage of the input–process–output model. It interfaces with input sensors and output devices via its I/O pins:

  • Input interfacing — a sensor (LDR, thermistor, microswitch) connects to an input pin. The microcontroller reads the voltage at that pin and compares it to a threshold in its program. For analogue sensors, an internal analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) converts the continuously varying voltage to a number the processor can use.
  • Output interfacing — output pins switch devices on or off. Because a microcontroller’s output pins can only supply small currents (typically 20–40 mA), high-power devices such as motors must be controlled via a transistor or relay, which acts as a switch that the microcontroller triggers.

Programs running on microcontrollers are made more efficient using sub-routines. Instead of writing the same sequence of instructions every time a task is needed, the programmer writes the instructions once as a sub-routine and calls it whenever required. For example, a “sound alarm” sub-routine that pulses a buzzer three times could be called from many different points in the program — when temperature exceeds a limit, when a door opens, or when a battery runs low — without rewriting the buzzer code each time.

A macro is a shorthand label assigned to a frequently used sequence of instructions. In block-based or flow-chart programming environments (common in schools), macros allow students to group a set of actions under one name and use it as a single step. Both sub-routines and macros reduce the length and complexity of programs, making them easier to test, debug and modify.

Benefits of Reprogrammable Systems

The ability to reprogram a microcontroller after the product is assembled brings several practical advantages that examiners expect students to explain with product context:

  • Flexibility — the same hardware can be used in different products simply by changing the program. A manufacturer can produce one PCB design and program it differently for a bedroom alarm clock and a kitchen timer.
  • Firmware updates — faults discovered after a product ships can be corrected by updating the program over a network or via a USB connection, without recalling and physically modifying the hardware.
  • Reduced component count — one microcontroller replaces many discrete components (comparators, counters, timers), reducing board size, material cost and assembly time.
  • Faster prototyping — engineers can write, test and refine the control logic rapidly without soldering new components. This shortens the development cycle and reduces waste.
Key Fact

Programmable systems can be updated after manufacture by changing the software, with no change to the physical circuit. This is a major commercial advantage: it reduces tooling costs, enables bug fixes without product recalls, and allows one hardware design to serve multiple product variants.

Limitations of Programmable Components

Microcontrollers are not always the best choice. Students must be able to evaluate both sides:

  • Programming expertise required — writing reliable control software demands skill. Bugs in the code can cause dangerous malfunctions in safety-critical products.
  • Higher unit cost for simple tasks — for a product that only ever needs to do one thing (such as a simple on/off switch), a fixed resistor-transistor circuit is cheaper and more reliable than a microcontroller.
  • Power consumption — a microcontroller consumes more power than a simple passive circuit, which matters in battery-powered products where runtime is critical.
  • Software dependency — if the program is corrupted (e.g. by a power surge during programming), the product fails entirely. A purely hardware circuit has no software to corrupt.

Microcontrollers are embedded in a huge range of everyday products. A modern washing machine uses a microcontroller to time wash cycles, monitor water temperature via a thermistor, detect an unbalanced drum via an accelerometer, and control the motor speed — all in a single chip. Without reprogrammability, manufacturers would need to produce different circuit boards for each wash programme (delicates, cottons, quick wash) instead of a single board with different software settings.

In Design and Technology projects, PICs are commonly programmed using block-based visual environments such as Flowcode or PicAxe BASIC. These tools generate machine code from a visual flowchart or simple text commands, making programming accessible without requiring advanced software engineering skills. The logic the student builds in the flowchart maps directly onto the sub-routine structure described in this lesson.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain’ and ‘Discuss’ questions on programmable systems, always embed a product context — “a microcontroller in a washing machine can be reprogrammed to fix a fault after sale, avoiding a costly recall” scores far more than “programmable systems can be updated.” For 8-mark discuss questions, make sure you include genuine limitations as well as benefits; a one-sided answer cannot reach the top mark band regardless of how well the advantages are developed.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A microcontroller (including PIC types) contains a processor, memory and I/O pins on a single chip, and can be programmed to control a wide range of electronic products.
  • Sub-routines and macros allow complex programs to be built from reusable sections of code, reducing length and making programs easier to test and update.
  • Key benefits of reprogrammable systems include flexibility, firmware updates and reduced component count; limitations include programming expertise needed, higher cost for simple tasks and power consumption.

practice_questions.text:
What does PIC stand for in the context of electronic systems?
A) Printed Interface Circuit
B) Programmable Interface Controller
C) Passive Input Component
D) Processed Integrated Circuit
practice_questions.marks: B) Programmable Interface Controller [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two components found inside a microcontroller.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per correct component named, up to 2. Accept: processor/CPU; memory (flash/RAM); input/output pins. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what a sub-routine is and explain why programmers use them.
practice_questions.marks:
• A sub-routine is a self-contained section of program code that performs a specific task. [1 mark]
• It can be called (used) from multiple points within the main program. [1 mark]
• This avoids repeating the same code, making programs shorter, easier to read and simpler to update. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a microcontroller's output pin cannot directly drive a motor and describe how this problem is solved.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A microcontroller's output pin can supply only a small current (around 20 to 40 mA), which is insufficient to drive a motor. [1 mark]
• A motor requires a much larger current to produce useful torque. [1 mark]
• A transistor or relay is connected between the output pin and the motor. [1 mark]
• The small current from the pin switches the transistor/relay on, which then allows the larger motor current to flow from a separate power supply. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A company manufactures a programmable security alarm that uses a microcontroller. Explain the advantages to the manufacturer of using a programmable system rather than a fixed circuit for this product.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The same circuit board can be programmed differently to produce a basic domestic alarm or a more complex commercial system, reducing tooling and manufacturing costs.
• Faults discovered after the product ships can be corrected by a software update rather than a product recall, saving significant cost.
• New features (e.g. an additional motion sensor input) can be added by updating the program without redesigning the hardware.
• The microcontroller replaces many discrete components, reducing board size and assembly time, which lowers unit cost.
[6 marks - Mastering: Three or more advantages with product-specific context developed. Secure: Two advantages with context. Developing: Two advantages named but context limited. Emerging: One advantage stated without development.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using a microcontroller rather than a fixed electronic circuit in a battery-powered children's toy.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
• The same toy can be updated with new sound effects or behaviours by reprogramming the microcontroller, extending the product's life without physical changes.
• One microcontroller replaces multiple discrete components, reducing board size and material cost, which is important in a price-sensitive toy market.
• If a programming fault causes the toy to behave incorrectly, a firmware update can fix it without recalling the product.
Disadvantages:
• A microcontroller consumes more power than a simple passive circuit, reducing battery life — a significant issue in a toy used by children who may forget to switch it off.
• Programming requires expertise; errors in the code could cause unexpected behaviour that might be perceived as a safety risk in a toy aimed at young children.
• For very simple functions (e.g. a sound that plays when a button is pressed), a fixed buzzer circuit would be cheaper and more reliable than a programmed microcontroller.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion, at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages with battery-powered toy context throughout. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited context. Emerging: Superficial or one-sided response.]

lessons.title: Mechanical Devices and Types of Motion
lessons.description: Rotary, linear, reciprocating and oscillating motion, and the devices that convert between them.
lessons.content_html:
Motion in Mechanical Systems

Mechanical systems convert one type of motion into another, or change the direction and magnitude of a force. Understanding the four types of motion is fundamental to analysing how any mechanism works — from a bicycle gearset to an industrial press. Before examining specific devices, you need to recognise and describe each motion type accurately, as exam questions often ask students to identify which motion is produced at a given point in a mechanism.

The Four Types of Motion

Rotary motion is circular movement around a fixed axis. Gears, wheels and motors all produce rotary motion. It is the most common type in powered machines because electric motors naturally produce rotation.

Linear motion is movement in a straight line. A drawer sliding in a cabinet, a piston being pushed along a cylinder, or a rack gear moving along a track are all examples of linear motion. Many mechanisms exist specifically to convert rotary motion (from a motor) into linear motion useful for the product’s function.

Reciprocating motion is backwards-and-forwards movement in a straight line. A jigsaw blade, a sewing machine needle and the pistons in a car engine all move with reciprocating motion. Reciprocating motion is often produced by converting rotary motion using a crank and slider mechanism.

Oscillating motion is a swinging or rocking movement — similar to reciprocating but following an arc rather than a straight line. A pendulum, a metronome and the escapement mechanism in a mechanical clock all exhibit oscillating motion.

Key Fact

The four types of motion are: rotary (circular), linear (straight line, one direction), reciprocating (straight line, back and forth) and oscillating (arc, back and forth). Distinguishing reciprocating from oscillating — both go ‘back and forth’ but reciprocating is along a straight line while oscillating follows a curved path — is a common exam trap.

Levers

A lever is a rigid bar that pivots about a fixed point called the fulcrum. Levers change the magnitude (size) of a force or its direction. The three classes of lever are defined by the positions of the effort, fulcrum and load:

  • First-order lever — fulcrum between effort and load. Changes direction of force. A seesaw and a pair of scissors are first-order levers.
  • Second-order lever — load between fulcrum and effort. Multiplies force (mechanical advantage > 1). A wheelbarrow is a second-order lever: the axle is the fulcrum, the load sits in the barrow, and the effort is applied at the handles.
  • Third-order lever — effort between fulcrum and load. Sacrifices force to gain speed or range of movement. Tweezers and a fishing rod are third-order levers.

A linkage is a set of rigid bars connected by pivots. Linkages transmit and transform motion within a mechanism. A reverse motion linkage has a fixed pivot in the centre of a bar; when one end moves up, the other moves down — used in bell-crank mechanisms and some vehicle steering systems. A parallel motion linkage keeps a bar horizontal as it moves, used in drawing boards, architect’s parallel rulers and pantograph mechanisms.

Linkages are lightweight, strong and simple to manufacture. They appear frequently in mechanisms that must redirect motion without the complexity of gears or electronics.

Gear Systems

Gears are toothed wheels that mesh together to transmit rotary motion. They change speed, torque (turning force) and direction of rotation. The gear attached to the driving source (motor) is the driver gear; the gear it turns is the driven gear. The teeth on meshing gears must be the same size.

Key relationships in gear systems:

  • A large driven gear turns slower than the driver but with more torque — useful for lifting heavy loads (clock mechanisms, winches).
  • A small driven gear turns faster than the driver but with less torque — useful for speed (fan blades, model racing cars).
  • Two meshing gears rotate in opposite directions. An idler gear placed between them makes the driven gear rotate in the same direction as the driver.

A rack and pinion converts rotary motion to linear motion. The circular pinion gear meshes with a flat toothed rack; as the pinion rotates, the rack slides in a straight line. Car steering systems, adjustable office chairs and the quill on a pillar drill all use rack-and-pinion mechanisms.

Bevel gears have angled teeth and mesh at right angles (or other angles), changing the axis of rotation by 90°. A hand-powered drill uses bevel gears to convert horizontal handle rotation into vertical drill rotation.

A worm drive has a helical screw (worm) meshing with a worm gear. The worm can only drive the gear — the gear cannot back-drive the worm — making this ideal for self-locking mechanisms such as guitar tuning pegs. Worm drives produce very high gear ratios in a compact space.

Cams and Followers

A cam is an off-centre rotating disc. A follower rests on the cam’s surface and rises and falls as the cam rotates, converting rotary motion into reciprocating or oscillating motion. Cam shape determines the follower’s movement pattern:

  • Snail (drop) cam — produces a slow rise followed by a sudden drop. Used in escapements and alarm mechanisms.
  • Eccentric (circular offset) cam — produces a smooth, regular rise and fall. Used in engine valve systems.
  • Pear-shaped cam — produces a long dwell (pause) at top and bottom, with rapid rise and fall. Used in sewing machines to control the needle action.
Key Fact

The rack and pinion converts rotary to linear motion. A cam and follower converts rotary to reciprocating motion. Gears and pulleys transmit and modify rotary motion without changing its type. Being able to state the motion conversion is a one-mark gain in most exam questions on mechanisms.

Pulley Systems

Pulleys use a belt or chain running over one or more grooved wheels to transmit rotary motion over a distance. Unlike gears (which mesh directly), pulleys rely on friction between the belt and the pulley groove to transmit force. This means friction is required for the mechanism to work — a common misconception is that friction is always undesirable. Without sufficient friction, the belt slips and power is lost. Pulley systems are widely used to transmit drive from motors to conveyor belts, lathes and washing machine drums.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When an exam question asks you to identify the type of motion at a point in a mechanism, look at the shape of the path: circular = rotary, straight line (one direction) = linear, straight line back and forth = reciprocating, arc back and forth = oscillating. For questions about gear or pulley systems, always state whether the driven component is faster or slower than the driver, and whether torque increases or decreases. A complete answer names the motion type AND describes the change in speed or force — neither alone is worth full marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four types of motion are rotary (circular), linear (straight line, one way), reciprocating (straight line, back and forth) and oscillating (arc, back and forth).
  • Rack and pinion converts rotary to linear motion; cams and followers convert rotary to reciprocating motion; gears and pulleys transmit and modify rotary motion.
  • Pulleys require friction between the belt and wheel to function; gears mesh directly via teeth. Both systems can change speed and torque, and the gear/pulley ratio determines by how much.

practice_questions.text: A designer is choosing between a gear system and a belt-and-pulley system to drive the drum of a washing machine from an electric motor. Compare the two systems, discussing their suitability for this application.
practice_questions.marks:
Gear system:
• Gears mesh directly via teeth; no slip possible — positive drive, reliable speed ratio.
• More expensive to manufacture with high precision; noisier in operation.
• Suitable where exact speed ratios must be maintained.
Belt-and-pulley system:
• Relies on friction between belt and pulley; can slip if overloaded (acts as safety release).
• Cheaper, quieter, and able to transmit drive over longer distances between shafts.
• Belts can stretch or snap over time — maintenance required.
• Most domestic washing machines use a belt drive because it is quieter and cheaper; the slip under overload protects the motor.
[5 marks — 1 mark per developed comparison point up to 5. A fully developed answer must address both systems with context of the washing machine.]

glossary_terms.definition: Circular movement around a central axis, such as a spinning gear or wheel.
Straight-line movement in one direction, such as a drawer sliding in and out.
Backwards and forwards movement along a straight line, such as the blade of a jigsaw.
A swinging or rocking movement back and forth, like a pendulum or a metronome.
A system of rigid bars or rods connected by pivot joints to transmit and transform movement between parts of a mechanism.
A mechanism using a round gear (pinion) meshing with a flat, toothed bar (rack) to convert rotary motion into linear motion.
An eccentric (off-centre) rotating disc that converts rotary motion into reciprocating or oscillating motion via a follower resting on its surface.

lessons.title: Mechanical Calculations: Levers, Gears and Pulleys
lessons.description: Step-by-step worked examples for mechanical advantage, gear ratio and velocity ratio calculations.
lessons.content_html:
Why Calculations Matter in Mechanisms

Mechanical calculations allow engineers to predict exactly how much force a lever can generate, how fast a driven gear will spin, or how many times a pulley system multiplies an effort. In the exam, calculation questions require you to state the formula, substitute values and give a numerical answer with correct units — a formula alone scores zero. This lesson works through each calculation type fully before you practise, following the same method every time.

Mechanical Advantage

Mechanical advantage (MA) tells us how much a mechanism multiplies a force. A mechanical advantage greater than 1 means the mechanism amplifies the effort; less than 1 means the mechanism sacrifices force to gain speed or range.

The formula is:

$$\text{MA} = \frac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$$

For levers, MA can also be calculated from distances if force values are not given:

$$\text{MA} = \frac{\text{distance from fulcrum to effort}}{\text{distance from fulcrum to load}}$$

A first-order lever has its fulcrum 0.2 m from the load and 0.8 m from the effort. Calculate the mechanical advantage.

Step 1 — Write the formula:

$$\text{MA} = \frac{\text{distance from fulcrum to effort}}{\text{distance from fulcrum to load}}$$

Step 2 — Substitute values:

$$\text{MA} = \frac{0.8}{0.2}$$

Step 3 — Calculate and state answer:

$$\text{MA} = 4$$

The lever has a mechanical advantage of 4. This means an effort of 5 N would lift a load of 20 N. Note: MA has no units — it is a pure ratio.

The Principle of Moments

The principle of moments states that for a lever in equilibrium (balanced), the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment. A moment is the turning effect of a force about a pivot.

$$\text{Moment} = \text{Force} \times \text{perpendicular distance from pivot}$$

Units: Newton-metres (Nm). Force is in newtons (N) and distance is in metres (m).

A uniform lever is balanced on a fulcrum. A 60 N load sits 0.3 m from the fulcrum on the left. What effort must be applied 0.9 m from the fulcrum on the right to keep the lever balanced?

Step 1 — Write the principle of moments:

$$\text{Clockwise moment} = \text{Anticlockwise moment}$$

Step 2 — Substitute:

$$\text{Effort} \times 0.9 = 60 \times 0.3$$

Step 3 — Solve:

$$\text{Effort} = \frac{60 \times 0.3}{0.9} = \frac{18}{0.9} = 20 \text{ N}$$

An effort of 20 N is required. The lever gives a mechanical advantage of 3 (60 ÷ 20), confirming the longer effort arm tripled the force.

Key Fact

Moment (Nm) = Force (N) × perpendicular distance from pivot (m). The longer the effort arm, the smaller the effort needed to balance a given load — this is why a long spanner undoes a tight bolt more easily than a short one.

Gear Ratio

The gear ratio compares the number of teeth on the driven gear to those on the driver gear:

$$\text{Gear ratio} = \frac{\text{teeth on driven gear}}{\text{teeth on driver gear}}$$

A driver gear has 12 teeth. The driven gear has 48 teeth. The driver turns at 200 rpm. Calculate the gear ratio and the output speed of the driven gear.

Step 1 — Gear ratio:

$$\text{Gear ratio} = \frac{48}{12} = 4:1$$

Step 2 — Output speed:

$$\text{Output speed} = \frac{\text{Input speed}}{\text{Gear ratio}} = \frac{200}{4} = 50 \text{ rpm}$$

The driven gear turns at 50 rpm — four times slower than the driver, but with four times the torque. A 4:1 ratio is described as a step-down (reduction) gear. Always include units (rpm) in your final answer.

Velocity Ratio of Pulley Systems

In a belt-and-pulley system, the velocity ratio (VR) compares pulley diameters. Because both pulleys share the same belt, the belt travels at the same linear speed at both pulleys:

$$\text{VR} = \frac{\text{diameter of driven pulley}}{\text{diameter of driver pulley}}$$

The output speed of the driven pulley is:

$$\text{Output speed} = \frac{\text{Input speed}}{\text{VR}}$$

A motor drives a 50 mm diameter pulley (driver) connected by a belt to a 200 mm diameter pulley (driven). The motor runs at 1 200 rpm. Calculate the velocity ratio and output speed.

Step 1 — Velocity ratio:

$$\text{VR} = \frac{200}{50} = 4$$

Step 2 — Output speed:

$$\text{Output speed} = \frac{1200}{4} = 300 \text{ rpm}$$

The driven pulley turns at 300 rpm. As with gears, a larger driven pulley gives a slower but more powerful (higher torque) output. Remember: for this to work, the belt must not slip — friction between belt and pulley is essential.

Key Fact

Gear ratio and pulley velocity ratio both use the same structure: driven ÷ driver. A ratio greater than 1 means the output is slower with more torque (step-down). A ratio less than 1 means the output is faster with less torque (step-up). Always state the formula, show working, and include units in the final answer.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 3-mark ‘Calculate’ questions, always use three clear steps: (1) write the formula, (2) substitute the numbers, (3) calculate and box the final answer with units. A correct formula with no answer scores zero. For lever questions involving the principle of moments, check whether the question gives you forces or distances — both can appear. MA has no units; moments are in Nm; speed is in rpm. Confusing these units is the most common error in calculation questions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort (or effort arm ÷ load arm for levers). The principle of moments states that clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments at equilibrium.
  • Gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth; velocity ratio = driven diameter ÷ driver diameter. Both determine whether output speed increases or decreases relative to the input.
  • Always state the formula, substitute values and give a boxed final answer with correct units. MA is unitless; moments are in Nm; speed is in rpm; force is in N.

practice_questions.text:
A lever has its fulcrum 0.1 m from the load and 0.5 m from the effort. What is the mechanical advantage of this lever?
A) 0.2
B) 2
C) 5
D) 50
State the formula used to calculate the gear ratio of a pair of meshing gears.
practice_questions.marks: Gear ratio = number of teeth on driven gear ÷ number of teeth on driver gear. [2 marks: 1 for identifying driven/driver correctly, 1 for correct ratio structure]

practice_questions.text: A driver gear with 20 teeth meshes with a driven gear with 60 teeth. The driver rotates at 300 rpm. Calculate the gear ratio and the output speed of the driven gear. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Gear ratio = 60 ÷ 20 = 3:1 [1 mark for correct ratio]
Output speed = 300 ÷ 3 = 100 rpm [1 mark for correct calculation, 1 mark for units (rpm)] [3 marks total]

practice_questions.text: A lever is balanced on a fulcrum. A 90 N load is placed 0.2 m from the fulcrum. Calculate the effort required at a point 0.6 m from the fulcrum on the other side to keep the lever in equilibrium. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Principle of moments: Effort × 0.6 = 90 × 0.2 [1 mark for correct equation setup]
Effort × 0.6 = 18
Effort = 18 ÷ 0.6 = 30 N [1 mark for correct calculation, 1 mark for units (N)] [3 marks total]

practice_questions.text: A belt-and-pulley system has a driver pulley of 40 mm diameter and a driven pulley of 160 mm diameter. The driver runs at 800 rpm. Calculate the velocity ratio and the output speed of the driven pulley. Explain what happens to the torque as a result of this ratio.
practice_questions.marks:
VR = 160 ÷ 40 = 4 [1 mark]
Output speed = 800 ÷ 4 = 200 rpm [1 mark for calculation, 1 mark for units]
Torque increases by a factor of 4 at the output [1 mark]
Explanation: a larger driven pulley turns more slowly but provides greater turning force [1 mark]
Application: this principle is used in washing machine drum drives where high torque is needed to agitate heavy wet laundry at low drum speed [1 mark]
[6 marks — Mastering: All calculation steps correct, torque effect explained with product context. Secure: Calculation correct, torque direction stated without full explanation. Developing: VR correct but output speed or torque explanation incomplete. Emerging: Formula stated but substitution or calculation incorrect.]

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating a manual can opener. The turning handle has an effort arm of 80 mm from the pivot and the cutting blade is attached 20 mm from the pivot. Calculate the mechanical advantage. Evaluate whether this design is suitable for a person with reduced grip strength and suggest one specific modification to improve it.
practice_questions.marks:
Calculation:
MA = 80 ÷ 20 = 4 [2 marks: 1 formula, 1 correct answer]
Evaluation:
• MA of 4 means the user applies four times less force than the cutting force, which reduces the effort needed — suitable for most users but may still require significant grip strength. [2 marks]
• A person with reduced grip strength may still struggle if the friction from the can rim or dull blade adds resistance not captured in the MA calculation alone. [2 marks]
• The handle diameter and texture also affect comfort — a thin hard handle concentrates force on the palm, increasing discomfort. [1 mark]
Modification:
• Increase the effort arm to, e.g., 160 mm — doubling it to give MA = 8, halving the required effort. [1 mark]
• OR fit a soft ergonomic grip to spread contact force across a wider palm area. [1 mark]
• OR add a ratchet mechanism so continuous rotation is not required, reducing peak grip force. [1 mark]
[10 marks — Mastering: Correct calculation, sustained evaluation addressing suitability and limitations with quantified evidence, specific justified modification. Secure: Correct calculation, basic suitability evaluation, modification stated. Developing: Partial calculation or evaluation without modification. Emerging: Attempt at calculation only.]

lessons.title: Forces, Stresses and Reinforcement
lessons.description: Tension, compression, torsion, shear and bending — and how structures are reinforced against each.
lessons.content_html:
Forces in Structures and Products

Every physical product experiences forces during its use — the weight of books compresses a shelf, a twisted door handle experiences torsion, and a loaded bridge beam bends under traffic. Designers must understand the nature of these forces so they can choose the right material, shape and reinforcement strategy to ensure the product survives its intended service life without failing. Exam questions on this topic expect you to identify the type of stress acting on a component and justify a reinforcement choice with material and structural reasoning.

The Five Types of Stress

Tension is a pulling or stretching force. When two forces act along the same axis in opposite directions, pulling the material apart, the material is in tension. Examples: a rope suspending a load, a chain on a bicycle, the bottom flange of a loaded beam.

Compression is a pushing or squeezing force. When two forces act along the same axis pushing towards each other, the material is compressed and tends to shorten or buckle. Examples: the legs of a chair supporting a seated person, the columns of a building, the top flange of a loaded beam.

Torsion is a twisting force. When one end of a component is held fixed and a torque is applied to the other end, the material twists. A screwdriver shaft, a car drive shaft and a door handle spindle all experience torsion in normal use.

Shear is a cutting or sliding force where adjacent sections of a material tend to slide past each other. Scissors, chisels and bolts connecting structural members all experience shear. Shear is also the stress that causes a beam to fail by cracking vertically near its supports.

Bending occurs when a force acts perpendicular to the long axis of a component, causing it to curve. The top of a bent beam is in compression; the bottom is in tension. A shelf loaded at its centre, a diving board and a roof rafter all experience bending.

Key Fact

The five stresses are: tension (pulling apart), compression (pushing together), torsion (twisting), shear (sliding/cutting) and bending (top compressed, bottom stretched). A beam under a central load experiences both compression (top) and tension (bottom) simultaneously — this is a common exam question.

Reinforcement Methods by Material

Reinforcement increases a component’s resistance to failure without making it excessively heavy or expensive. Different material families use different structural techniques:

Papers and Boards

Corrugating paper creates a wavy internal layer that vastly increases bending stiffness. Corrugated cardboard packaging uses this principle: the fluted inner layer resists compression from the top surface, while the flat outer liners resist tension and provide a smooth printing surface. Without the corrugation, the same amount of paper would buckle under a fraction of the load.

Timbers

Laminating layers of wood (as in plywood or laminated veneer lumber) with the grain alternated at 90° distributes forces in multiple directions. A single piece of timber is strong along the grain but weak across it; plywood resists forces in both directions equally. Gussets — triangular corner reinforcements — are used at frame joints to resist racking (shear forces that push a rectangular frame into a parallelogram).

Metals

Metal sections can be formed into shapes that increase their second moment of area — effectively concentrating material away from the neutral axis to maximise resistance to bending. An I-beam (universal beam) is the classic example: the flanges are far from the centre, giving very high bending resistance with minimal material. Ribs on metal enclosures (such as those on the inside of cast aluminium gear housings) perform the same function, resisting bending while keeping the wall thin and light. Hollow box sections resist both bending and torsion more efficiently than solid sections of the same mass.

Polymers

Polymers are often reinforced at points of weakness using additional wall thickness, ribbing on the inside of moulded parts, or by embedding them in a matrix of fibres. Ribs on the inside of an injection-moulded plastic casing resist bending without increasing the outer wall thickness (which would cause sink marks and extend cooling time). Glass-reinforced polymer (GRP) uses glass fibres within a polyester resin matrix; the fibres resist tension that the resin alone could not withstand.

When a beam bends, stress is highest at the top (compression) and bottom (tension) surfaces and nearly zero at the neutral axis in the middle. An I-beam exploits this by placing the majority of its material at the flanges (top and bottom), where stress is highest, and using only a thin web in the middle where stress is low. The same mass of steel in a rectangular section would be far weaker in bending because much of the material sits near the neutral axis doing little structural work.

This principle also explains why hollow tubes resist bending and torsion better than solid rods of the same cross-sectional area: material near the centre contributes little to resisting these forces. Bicycle frames use aluminium or carbon fibre tubes for exactly this reason — light, stiff and strong because the material is distributed at the outer surface where stresses are highest.

Textiles and Fibres

Interfacing is a woven or non-woven fabric bonded to the reverse of a textile to add stiffness — used in shirt collars, waistbands and the structured panels of bags. Webbing — tightly woven strips of nylon, polyester or polypropylene — is used for straps and harnesses because it has very high tensile strength along its length. Quilting (sandwiching insulation between fabric layers, held by stitching) resists delamination and maintains the insulating layer’s thickness under repeated compression.

Key Fact

Reinforcement works by distributing stress over a larger area or redirecting it into a form the material can withstand. Corrugating (paper/boards), laminating (timber), ribbing and I-section profiles (metals), ribbing inside moulded parts (polymers) and interfacing/webbing (textiles) are all exam-required reinforcement techniques. Know at least one technique per material family.

The most common error in exam answers on this topic is confusing bending with compression. A shelf that sags in the middle is bending, not simply compressing — the top surface is in compression and the bottom is in tension. Stating only “the shelf is compressed by the books” misses the structure of the stress and will only score partial marks.

A second common error is describing reinforcement too vaguely. “Make it thicker” is not a reinforcement technique — it simply adds material without changing the distribution of stress. A specific answer names the structural form: “adding ribs to the inside of the moulded casing increases bending stiffness without increasing wall thickness, avoiding sink marks in the surface finish.” This level of specificity is required for the top mark band on applied questions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions asking you to identify the type of stress acting on a component, look at the direction and effect of the force: pulling apart = tension; pushing together = compression; twisting = torsion; sliding = shear; curving the component = bending. For questions asking you to ‘justify’ a reinforcement method, name the technique (corrugating, ribbing, laminating, etc.), state which stress it resists and explain the structural reason — not just “it makes it stronger.” A 6-mark explain answer that names a material-specific technique and explains the mechanism of reinforcement will reach the Secure band or above.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five stresses are tension (pull), compression (push), torsion (twist), shear (slide/cut) and bending (top compressed, bottom stretched). A beam under a central load experiences both compression and tension simultaneously.
  • Reinforcement techniques are material-specific: corrugating (paper/boards), laminating (timber), ribs and I-sections (metals/polymers), interfacing and webbing (textiles).
  • Effective reinforcement redistributes stress over a larger area or concentrates material where stress is highest — not just adding thickness throughout.

practice_questions.text:
A bicycle chain is pulled tight between the pedal gear and the rear wheel gear while the cyclist pedals. What type of stress is the chain experiencing?
A) Compression
B) Torsion
C) Tension
D) Shear
practice_questions.marks: C) Tension [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the type of stress acting on the top surface of a wooden shelf that sags under the weight of heavy books.
practice_questions.marks: Compression. [1 mark] (The top of a bent beam/shelf is in compression; the bottom is in tension. Accept 'bending' as the overall stress type with 'compression at the top surface' for full credit.)

practice_questions.text: Describe how corrugating a sheet of card increases its resistance to bending.
practice_questions.marks:
• The corrugated layer creates a wavy internal structure with peaks and troughs. [1 mark]
• The vertical elements of the corrugation resist compressive forces acting from above. [1 mark]
• This increases the card's stiffness under bending loads without significantly increasing the material mass. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain why an I-beam profile resists bending forces more efficiently than a solid rectangular section of the same mass of steel.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• When a beam bends, stress is highest at the top (compression) and bottom (tension) surfaces and nearly zero at the neutral axis in the centre. [1 mark]
• An I-beam concentrates its material in the flanges at the top and bottom, where bending stress is highest. [1 mark]
• The thin web in the middle carries little of the bending load, so placing material there (as a solid section does) is structurally inefficient. [1 mark]
• The same mass of steel in an I-section therefore provides far greater bending resistance than a solid rectangular section. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating a rigid shoulder bag from a woven cotton fabric. Explain, with reference to specific reinforcement techniques, how the structural integrity of the bag can be improved so that it withstands tension in the strap and prevents the base from deforming under load.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Nylon or polypropylene webbing should be used for the shoulder strap because webbing has very high tensile strength along its length and will resist the tension created by the weight of the bag's contents. [2 marks]
• Interfacing bonded to the base panel adds rigidity, distributing the compressive and bending forces from the loaded bag contents over a wider area rather than allowing the fabric to deform. [2 marks]
• Reinforced stitching at stress concentration points — where the strap attaches to the bag body — distributes shear forces that would otherwise cause the strap to tear out. [1 mark]
• An internal base board or rigid panel can be inserted to resist the shear and bending loads at the base. [1 mark]
[6 marks — Mastering: Three techniques named with material-specific justification linked to the specific stress type each resists. Secure: Two techniques with justification. Developing: One technique named with basic explanation. Emerging: Vague suggestion ('make it stronger') without technique or stress type.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using glass-reinforced polymer (GRP) compared to sheet aluminium for the bodywork panels of a sports car.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of GRP over sheet aluminium:
• GRP can be formed into complex double-curvature shapes (such as curved body panels) without the expensive tooling and pressing equipment required to shape aluminium.
• GRP has a lower density than aluminium (approximately 1.8 g/cm³ vs 2.7 g/cm³), reducing the vehicle's overall mass and improving performance.
• GRP does not corrode, reducing maintenance requirements and extending panel life in wet climates.
• GRP panels can be repaired with filler and resin without specialist equipment; dented aluminium panels often require panel beating and repainting.
Disadvantages of GRP:
• GRP has lower stiffness than aluminium for the same thickness; panels may flex or vibrate at high speed unless additional thickness or ribbing is added.
• GRP is more difficult to recycle at end of life; thermoset resins cannot be remelted, whereas aluminium is highly recyclable.
• GRP is more flammable than aluminium and may release toxic fumes if the vehicle catches fire.
• Surface finish on GRP requires gel-coat application and careful mould preparation; aluminium can be anodised or painted directly.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages specific to sports car bodywork. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development, limited balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]

glossary_terms.definition: A pulling force acting along the length of a material, stretching it.
A squeezing or pushing force that acts to shorten a material along its length.
A twisting force applied around the long axis of a material.
A force that causes one part of a material to slide relative to an adjacent part, like scissors cutting through paper.
A force that creates a combination of tension and compression across the cross-section of a material, causing it to curve.
A manufacturing technique that forms a material into a series of parallel folds or waves, significantly increasing stiffness without adding weight.
The bonding of thin layers of material together with grain directions alternated, increasing strength and reducing the tendency to warp.
Structural ridges or walls added to a surface to resist bending without adding solid thickness.
A stiff material bonded to a fabric layer to increase its structural rigidity and resistance to deformation.
